decision-making.description: Trial structure of a vignette-based framing task: imagine 600 people infected by a fatal disease, choose a sure option or a gamble, framed as lives saved (positive) or lives lost (negative); an Asian-disease-style framing task, related variant, not the exact CogLab questions.
decision-making.figureCaption: The vignette-based paradigm. At the beginning of each trial, the social problem with initial amount was shown for 4 s. The amount was a gain in the gain domain (A) and a loss in the loss domain (B). The participants were informed that the social problem with initial amount may or may not happen, depending on their subsequent choices. Then a sure option was shown on the left of the screen and a gambling option was shown on the right of the screen for 6 s. The sure option was presented in a positive frame or negative frame in both domains, while a gambling option was depicted as the frequency of a successful outcome or losing. Participants were asked to make a decision within 6 s without feedback.

monty-hall.description: Schematic of the Monty Hall dilemma: pick one of three doors, the host opens a non-prize door, then stick or switch; shows correct (2/3) versus incorrect (1/2) reasoning. Schematic of the task from a review/perspective article, not the CogLab simulation.
monty-hall.figureCaption: Schematic representation of the MHD with the host (top) and player (bottom). (1) A player is presented three doors, each with an equal chance (1/3) of containing a prize and he chooses one of them. (2) Following the initial selection, the player now has one door with a 1/3 chance of having the prize. The host now has two doors with a total 2/3 chance of having the prize (1/3 + 1/3). (3) The host opens one of his two doors which does not contain the prize. The player is offered the choice to stick with his original selection or to switch to the unopened door held by the host. (4a) Correct Reasoning: Given that the opening of a non-rewarding door is obligatory, there still remains a 2/3 chance that the prize is on the "side" of the host, and a 1/3 chance that the prize is behind the player's originally chosen door. (4b) Incorrect Reasoning: A typical cognitive error is based on the illusion of equiprobability between the two remaining doors.

risky-decisions.figureCaption: The financial decision-making task. Participants were told that they would first receive an initial amount. Second, they were instructed that they would not be able to retain the entire initial amount and would have to chose between a sure and a risky option.
